questions.text: Which federal law primarily governs the privacy and security of protected health information (PHI) in the United States?
questions.explanation: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) is the primary federal law governing the privacy and security of protected health information. The HITECH Act strengthened HIPAA enforcement but HIPAA is the foundational law.

questions.text: A healthcare organization wants to compare its patient fall rate to that of similar hospitals nationally. This process is best described as:
questions.explanation: Benchmarking is the process of comparing an organization's performance data against external standards, best practices, or similar organizations to identify performance gaps and opportunities for improvement.

questions.text: In healthcare data management, 'data validity' refers to:

options.a: How quickly data can be retrieved from the EHR system
options.b: Whether data accurately measures what it is intended to measure
options.c: The number of data points collected in a given period
options.d: The frequency with which data is updated in the system

questions.explanation: Data validity (or accuracy) ensures that the data collected truly represents what it claims to measure. Invalid data can lead to incorrect conclusions and poor quality decisions.

questions.text: A hospital is implementing a new EHR system. Which of the following is the MOST important consideration for patient safety?

options.a: Ensuring the vendor offers the lowest possible cost
options.b: Completing implementation as quickly as possible
options.c: Providing thorough staff training and testing before go-live
options.d: Decommissioning the old system immediately at go-live

questions.explanation: EHR implementations carry significant patient safety risks if staff are not properly trained. Thorough training and testing before go-live reduces medication errors, workflow disruptions, and data integrity issues.

questions.text: Which type of data is MOST useful for identifying trends in patient outcomes over time?

options.a: Cross-sectional data collected at a single point in time
options.b: Longitudinal data collected repeatedly over an extended period
options.c: Qualitative data from patient focus groups
options.d: Anecdotal data from staff incident reports

questions.explanation: Longitudinal data, collected over time for the same patients or processes, is most effective for identifying trends, measuring the impact of interventions, and predicting future outcomes.
